title: Moses' Final Charge
overview: Deuteronomy 31 marks a pivotal moment in Israel’s history as Moses prepares to pass leadership to Joshua and encourages the people to remain faithful to God’s covenant. At 120 years old, Moses acknowledges his impending death and inability to enter the Promised Land. God reassures Israel of His continued presence and promises victory over their enemies. Moses writes down the law, instructing its public reading every seven years to ensure the people’s obedience. The chapter also introduces a prophetic warning about Israel’s future unfaithfulness and the consequences of turning to foreign gods. A song is composed as a witness against Israel’s rebellion, highlighting the seriousness of covenant faithfulness. This chapter bridges the leadership transition and sets the stage for Israel’s entrance into Canaan, emphasizing God’s faithfulness and the necessity of courage and obedience.
structure:
**Verses 1-8: Moses’ Farewell and Encouragement.** Moses announces his age and impending death, reminding Israel that God will lead them into the Promised Land through Joshua. He exhorts both Israel and Joshua to be strong and courageous, assuring them of God’s unfailing presence.

**Verses 9-13: The Law to be Publicly Read.** Moses writes down the law and commands its reading every seven years during the Feast of Tabernacles, ensuring all—including women, children, and foreigners—hear and learn to fear and obey God.

**Verses 14-18: God’s Warning of Israel’s Future Rebellion.** God reveals to Moses that Israel will forsake Him after his death, provoking His anger and resulting in judgment, yet this also serves as a solemn warning.

**Verses 19-22: The Song as a Witness.** Moses is instructed to write a song that will serve as a testimony against Israel’s future disobedience, ensuring the covenant’s terms are remembered.

**Verses 23-30: Joshua’s Commission and Moses’ Final Instructions.** Moses charges Joshua to lead Israel courageously into the land. He places the law beside the ark as a witness and warns the leaders of Israel about their rebellion and the consequences after his death, concluding with the public recitation of the song.

keyVerses.text: Be strong and of a good courage, fear not, nor be afraid of them: for the LORD thy God, he it is that doth go with thee; he will not fail thee, nor forsake thee.
keyVerses.significance: This verse encapsulates the chapter’s central encouragement to Israel and Joshua, emphasizing God’s faithful presence as the foundation for courage and obedience in the face of challenges.

keyVerses.text: And the LORD said unto Moses, Behold, thy days approach that thou must die: call Joshua, and present yourselves in the tabernacle of the congregation, that I may give him a charge. And Moses and Joshua went, and presented themselves in the tabernacle of the congregation.
keyVerses.significance: God’s direct revelation to Moses about his impending death and the commissioning of Joshua highlights the divine authority behind the leadership transition and the continuity of God’s plan.

keyVerses.text: Now therefore write ye this song for you, and teach it the children of Israel: put it in their mouths, that this song may be a witness for me against the children of Israel.
keyVerses.significance: The song serves as a prophetic and covenantal witness, designed to remind Israel of their responsibilities and the consequences of disobedience, underscoring the seriousness of God’s covenant.

keyVerses.text: And he gave Joshua the son of Nun a charge, and said, Be strong and of a good courage: for thou shalt bring the children of Israel into the land which I sware unto them: and I will be with thee.
keyVerses.significance: This verse reiterates the call to Joshua to lead with courage and faith, assuring him of God’s presence as he fulfills the divine promise to Israel.

characters.name: Moses
characters.description: The aging leader of Israel who prepares the people for his death and the transition of leadership to Joshua. He writes the law, encourages Israel, and delivers God’s warnings about future rebellion.

characters.name: Joshua
characters.description: Moses’ appointed successor, commissioned to lead Israel into the Promised Land. He is exhorted to be strong and courageous, relying on God’s presence and promises.

characters.name: The LORD (God)
characters.description: The sovereign God who speaks directly to Moses, assures Israel of His presence, commands the writing of the law and song, and warns of Israel’s future unfaithfulness and its consequences.

themes.description: This chapter highlights the orderly transfer of leadership from Moses to Joshua, emphasizing God’s sovereignty in guiding His people and the importance of faithful leadership.
Repeated exhortations to be strong and courageous underscore the necessity of trusting God’s presence amidst uncertainty, a theme central to Israel’s identity and mission.

The chapter stresses the importance of obedience to God’s law, the public reading of the law, and warns of the consequences of covenant unfaithfulness, reflecting the covenantal framework of Israel’s relationship with God.
Despite Israel’s future failures, God’s promises remain sure, and His presence continues with His people, demonstrating His steadfast commitment to His covenant.

historicalContext: Deuteronomy 31 is set during the late Bronze Age, approximately the 15th century BC, as the Israelites prepare to enter Canaan after 40 years of wilderness wandering. The geography centers around the eastern side of the Jordan River, near the plains of Moab. The political context involves the imminent conquest of Canaanite nations under Joshua’s leadership. Ancient Near Eastern customs emphasized covenantal loyalty to deities, public law reading, and communal remembrance practices, all reflected in Moses’ instructions for periodic law reading and the use of a song as a covenant witness. The ark of the covenant symbolized God’s presence and served as a legal and spiritual focal point for Israel.

theologicalInterpretations.description: Reformed theology emphasizes God’s sovereign election and covenant faithfulness in this chapter, viewing Moses’ warnings as a sober reminder of human sinfulness and the necessity of grace. The call to courage rests on God’s unchanging promises.

Dispensationalists see this chapter as a transitional moment in God’s redemptive plan, with Joshua’s leadership foreshadowing Christ’s ultimate leadership. The warnings about Israel’s future apostasy highlight the distinction between Israel and the Church.

Early Church Fathers often interpreted the song and law as typologies of Christ’s teaching and the Church’s need to remain faithful. Moses’ commissioning of Joshua prefigures Christ’s sending of the apostles to lead God’s people.

crossReferences.connection: Joshua’s charge to be strong and courageous echoes Deuteronomy 31:6-8, reinforcing God’s promise to be with His people during leadership transitions.
This psalm reflects the importance of teaching God’s laws to the next generation, paralleling Moses’ command for the law’s public reading in Deuteronomy 31.
The author contrasts Moses and Jesus, highlighting the significance of faithful leadership and the fulfillment of God’s promises beyond Moses’ ministry.
Isaiah references a song used as a witness against Israel, similar to the song Moses writes in Deuteronomy 31 to testify against Israel’s future disobedience.
Paul’s teaching on Scripture’s role in instruction and correction aligns with Moses’ emphasis on the law’s public reading and teaching in this chapter.

application: Trust in God’s presence and promises when facing leadership changes or personal challenges.
Regularly engage with Scripture publicly and privately to grow in obedience and reverence for God.
Teach and model faithfulness to God’s commands to the next generation within families and communities.
Respond to God’s warnings with repentance and renewed commitment to covenant faithfulness.
Encourage and support leaders who faithfully shepherd God’s people, recognizing God’s hand upon their ministry.
conclusion: Deuteronomy 31 stands as a profound testament to God’s faithfulness amid human frailty and transition. Moses’ final charge to Israel and Joshua underscores the necessity of courage grounded in God’s abiding presence. The chapter’s emphasis on covenant obedience, public teaching of the law, and the prophetic song as a witness against future rebellion reminds believers of the enduring call to faithfulness. For Christians today, it encourages reliance on God’s promises, the importance of Scripture’s central place in community life, and the responsibility to pass faith to future generations with courage and conviction.
